217.title: Contains Duplicate
217.prompt: Decide whether any integer occurs more than once.
hints: Remember the values already processed.
A failed set insertion detects a repeated value.
217.approach: The set contains exactly the earlier values. If adding the current value returns false, an equal earlier value exists.
217.cost: Expected O(n) time and O(n) space.

242.title: Valid Anagram
242.prompt: Check whether two lowercase English strings contain identical letter multiplicities.
hints: Order is irrelevant but multiplicity matters.
Increment counts for one string and decrement for the other.
242.approach: Equal lengths and zero final differences in all 26 letter counts are equivalent to having the same multiset of letters.
242.cost: O(n) time and O(1) space for the fixed alphabet.

383.title: Ransom Note
383.prompt: Determine whether lowercase magazine letters can supply every letter in a ransom note, using each occurrence once.
hints: Count available letters rather than searching repeatedly.
Consuming a letter must never make its remaining count negative.
383.approach: Build the magazine inventory, then consume the note. A negative count identifies the first unsupplied occurrence.
383.cost: O(m+n) time. O(m+n) temporary char-array space in this implementation; the 26 counters themselves use O(1).

205.title: Isomorphic Strings
205.prompt: Determine whether characters can be consistently renamed from s to t with a one-to-one mapping.
205.example: egg / add → true; foo / bar → false
hints: Consistency in one direction is insufficient.
Record both forward and reverse mappings.
205.approach: Each aligned character pair must agree with both previously established mappings. The reverse map forbids two source characters from collapsing onto one target.
205.cost: Expected O(n) time and O(min(n, alphabet size)) space. Java char units are the symbols.

290.title: Word Pattern
290.prompt: Match each pattern character bijectively to one space-separated word.
290.example: pattern=abba, words="dog cat cat dog" → true
hints: A repeated pattern character must repeat the same word.
Also forbid different characters from claiming the same word.
290.approach: Maintain the forward mapping plus the set of already claimed words. Reject differing word counts before matching.
290.cost: Expected O(L) time and O(L) space including split strings, where L is total input length. Assumes single spaces as in the problem.

36.title: Valid Sudoku
36.prompt: Validate the filled cells of a 9×9 Sudoku board; dots are empty. Do not solve the puzzle.
36.example: Two 5s in the same row → false, even if the board is unfinished.
hints: Each filled digit belongs to three constraint groups.
Track seen digits separately for each row, column, and 3×3 box.
36.approach: A digit is legal only if unseen in all three groups. The box index (r/3)*3+c/3 gives a unique index from 0 to 8.
36.cost: O(1) time and space for a fixed 9×9 board (81 cells). Validation does not establish solvability.

219.title: Contains Duplicate II
219.prompt: Find equal array values at two different indices whose distance is at most k.
hints: Only the most recent occurrence of a value can minimize its distance to the current index.
Store value → latest index and check before updating.
219.approach: For a current value, the latest equal index is the closest earlier match. If it is too far away, all older matches are too far away too.
219.cost: Expected O(n) time and O(n) space. A bounded window set is an alternative with O(min(n,k)) space.

41.title: First Missing Positive
41.prompt: Find the smallest missing positive integer in linear time using constant extra space; input mutation is allowed.
hints: For length n, the answer lies in 1 through n+1.
Place each in-range value x at index x−1, guarding against duplicate swaps.
41.approach: Repeatedly swap in-range values into their home positions. Every successful swap fixes a value in its home slot; a duplicate already there ends the loop. The first incorrect slot reveals the missing number.
41.cost: O(n) time because every successful swap places a value in its final slot; O(1) extra space. Mutates the array.

380.title: Insert Delete GetRandom O(1)
380.prompt: Design a set with expected constant-time insert, removal, and uniformly random selection from existing values.
380.example: insert(1) → true; insert(1) → false; remove(1) → true
hints: An array supports random indexing but arbitrary deletion is costly.
Swap a removed value with the last element and update an index map.
380.approach: The list stores each present value exactly once, while the map stores its position. Swap-with-last deletion preserves this bijection, so a uniform random index chooses each value equally often.
380.cost: Expected O(1) per operation, with amortized array append; O(n) storage. getRandom is called only on a nonempty set.

271.title: Encode and Decode Strings
271.prompt: Encode a list of strings into one string and decode it losslessly, including empty strings and delimiter characters.
hints: A delimiter alone can also appear in the data.
Prefix each string with its length and a separator, then read exactly that many characters.
271.approach: Each record is decimalLength#payload. The decoder reads only the length header up to #, then skips exactly the declared number of Java char units; separators inside the payload are ordinary data.
271.cost: O(L+k log(M+1)) time and output space for total payload length L, k strings, maximum length M; length headers contribute the logarithmic term. Decoder assumes valid encoded input.

2013.title: Detect Squares
2013.prompt: Store integer points with duplicates and count axis-aligned squares having a query point as one corner.
hints: Choose a stored point on the same horizontal line as the query.
Its horizontal distance determines the two possible square heights; multiply corner frequencies.
2013.approach: For each other x-coordinate on the query row, the side length is fixed. Check both vertical directions and multiply the counts of the other three corners. The query corner need not be stored.
2013.cost: Expected O(1) add; expected O(u) count for u distinct x-coordinates on the query row; O(P) storage for distinct stored points. Counts fit int under the original operation limit.

149.title: Max Points on a Line
149.prompt: Find the largest number of distinct input points lying on a single straight line.
hints: Fix one anchor and group other points by direction.
Reduce integer direction pairs with gcd and normalize their signs; avoid floating-point slopes.
149.approach: For each anchor, equal normalized directions identify collinear points. Reducing dx,dy by their gcd and selecting one sign convention merges opposite directions on the same line.
149.cost: Expected O(n² log C) time including gcd for coordinate difference bound C; O(n) space. Distinct points and the original coordinate limits avoid zero gcd and subtraction overflow.

11.title: Container With Most Water
11.prompt: Choose two vertical lines that form the largest water container with the horizontal axis.
hints: The shorter line determines the container height.
Keeping that shorter line while reducing width cannot improve the area.
11.approach: Evaluate the endpoints, then discard the shorter line. Any container retaining it with an inward partner has no greater height and smaller width, so it cannot beat the area just considered.
11.cost: O(n) time and O(1) space. Area fits int under the original bounds.

125.title: Valid Palindrome
125.prompt: Check whether an ASCII string is a palindrome after ignoring non-alphanumeric characters and letter case.
125.example: "A man, a plan, a canal: Panama" → true
hints: Compare surviving characters from opposite ends.
Skip punctuation independently on both sides.
125.approach: After skipping irrelevant characters, the outer remaining pair must match. Removing a matching pair leaves the same question on the interior.
125.cost: O(n) time and O(1) space. The original input is printable ASCII; general Unicode normalization is a separate concern.

392.title: Is Subsequence
392.prompt: Check whether s can be obtained from t by deleting characters without changing the remaining order.
hints: Keep the next required character of s.
Whenever t matches that character, advance the required position.
392.approach: Taking the earliest available match leaves the largest possible suffix for all remaining characters. The scan succeeds if it matches every character of s.

26.title: Remove Duplicates from Sorted Array
26.prompt: Compact a sorted integer array in place so its first k entries contain each distinct value once; return k.
hints: The written prefix is the unique sequence so far.
Compare each read value with the last written value.
26.approach: Sorted duplicates are contiguous. Write a value only when it differs from the most recent retained value; write never overtakes read.
26.cost: O(n) time and O(1) extra space. Only the returned prefix is meaningful.

27.title: Remove Element
27.prompt: Remove every occurrence of val in place and return the length of the retained prefix.
hints: Maintain a write position for accepted elements.
Read every value, but write only those different from val.
27.approach: After reading a prefix, the written prefix contains exactly its non-val elements. Since write is never ahead of read, overwriting cannot destroy unprocessed input.
27.cost: O(n) time and O(1) space; preserves relative order of retained values.

80.title: Remove Duplicates from Sorted Array II
80.prompt: Compact a sorted array in place so each value appears at most twice; return the retained length.
hints: Compare with the retained prefix rather than original neighboring indices.
Once two slots are written, accept x only if it differs from the value two slots back.
80.approach: Sorted order makes the second-last retained value sufficient to detect whether two copies of x have already been kept.
80.cost: O(n) time and O(1) space. The same retained-prefix rule generalizes to at most k copies.

88.title: Merge Sorted Array
88.prompt: Merge sorted nums2 into nums1, which has trailing capacity; m and n are their meaningful lengths.
hints: Writing from the beginning would overwrite unread nums1 values.
Fill from the back using the larger remaining value.
88.approach: The largest unmerged value belongs in the last free slot. Filling backward preserves unread nums1 entries. Once nums2 is exhausted, any remaining nums1 prefix is already correct.
88.cost: O(m+n) time and O(1) extra space.

189.title: Rotate Array
189.prompt: Rotate an array right by k positions in place.
hints: Separate the final k elements from the preceding prefix.
Reverse the whole array, then reverse each of the two parts.
189.approach: Reversing all elements exchanges the two blocks but reverses each internally. Reversing both blocks again restores their internal order.
189.cost: O(n) time and O(1) space. Mutates input; normalizing k handles rotations larger than n.

31.title: Next Permutation
31.prompt: Rearrange values into the next lexicographically larger permutation, or the smallest ordering if none exists.
hints: Find the longest nonincreasing suffix.
Increase the preceding pivot minimally, then reverse the suffix into ascending order.
31.approach: The descending suffix is already maximal for its prefix. Swap the pivot with the rightmost larger value, the smallest possible increase, then minimize the remaining suffix.
31.cost: O(n) time and O(1) space; handles duplicates with non-strict suffix comparisons.

75.title: Sort Colors
75.prompt: Sort an array containing only 0, 1, and 2 in one pass with constant extra space.
hints: Partition the array into finished zeros, finished ones, unknown values, and finished twos.
After swapping a two with the unknown right edge, inspect the incoming value again.
75.approach: Maintain [0,low) as zeros, [low,mid) as ones, and (high,n) as twos. The unknown interval shrinks by classifying nums[mid].
75.cost: O(n) time and O(1) extra space; mutates the array.

151.title: Reverse Words in a String
151.prompt: Reverse word order, removing leading/trailing spaces and reducing internal spaces to one.
hints: Scan backward to find each word’s end.
Skip spaces, identify one complete word, and append it with one separator.
151.approach: A backward scan visits words in output order. Appending slices avoids a separate token array, while the output builder handles normalization.
151.cost: O(n) time and O(n) output/builder space.

58.title: Length of Last Word
58.prompt: Return the length of the final word in a string of words separated by spaces.
hints: Trailing spaces are not part of the last word.
Skip spaces from the end, then count until the preceding space.
58.approach: After removing the trailing-space region conceptually, the next maximal non-space run is exactly the last word.
58.cost: O(n) worst-case time and O(1) space.

42.title: Trapping Rain Water
42.prompt: Compute total rainwater trapped between unit-width nonnegative bars.
hints: Water at an index depends on the smaller of its tallest left and right boundaries.
The side with the smaller known boundary can be finalized immediately.
42.approach: Maintain left and right boundary maxima. Finalize the side with the smaller maximum, since the opposite side already supplies a boundary at least that high. Each position contributes boundary height minus its bar height.
42.cost: O(n) time and O(1) space. Prefix-max arrays or a monotonic stack provide alternative O(n)-space formulations.

438.title: Find All Anagrams in a String
438.prompt: Find every starting index where a lowercase substring is an anagram of p.
hints: Every candidate has exactly p.length characters.
Maintain 26 counts while adding on the right and removing the character leaving on the left.
438.approach: A fixed-width window is an anagram exactly when its frequency vector equals the target vector. Comparing 26 entries is constant work per position.
438.cost: O(|s|+|p|) time for a fixed alphabet; O(1) auxiliary space plus output.

424.title: Longest Repeating Character Replacement
424.prompt: Find the longest uppercase substring that can become one repeated letter using at most k replacements.
hints: For a fixed window, all characters except its most frequent letter must change.
Maintain counts, shrink when window length minus its maximum frequency exceeds k.
424.approach: The replacement cost is window length minus the largest count. Recomputing that maximum over 26 letters keeps the validity rule exact and easy to justify.
424.cost: O(26n)=O(n) time and O(1) space for uppercase English letters.

30.title: Substring with Concatenation of All Words
30.prompt: Find starts of substrings formed by concatenating all given equal-length words, each with its required multiplicity, in any order.
hints: Word length lets you move the window one whole word at a time.
Scan each character offset modulo word length, shrinking when one word is overrepresented.
30.approach: Each offset scan maintains a window of valid dictionary words. Unknown words reset it; excess copies shrink it. A window holding exactly the required word count must have the target multiset.
30.cost: Expected O((n+m)w) time including copied/hashed length-w substrings, for text length n and m words; O(uw) map-key space for u distinct words, plus output. Words are nonempty and equal length.

35.title: Search Insert Position
35.prompt: Return the index of target in a sorted distinct array, or its insertion position.
hints: This is a boundary search rather than an arbitrary-match search.
Find the first value greater than or equal to target.
35.approach: Keep the insertion boundary in [left,right]. A midpoint below target cannot be the boundary; a qualifying midpoint remains a candidate.
35.cost: O(log n) time and O(1) space; returning n is valid.

74.title: Search a 2D Matrix
74.prompt: Search a matrix with sorted rows where each row begins above the previous row’s last value.
hints: The row ordering makes the whole matrix one sorted sequence.
Convert flat index mid into row mid/cols and column mid%cols.
74.approach: Binary-search the virtual flattened array without copying it. The stronger between-row guarantee is what permits this conversion.
74.cost: O(log(RC)) time and O(1) space. Flattened indices fit int under the original bounds.

240.title: Search a 2D Matrix II
240.prompt: Search a matrix whose rows and columns are independently sorted ascending.
hints: A top-right corner is largest in its row and smallest in its column.
If it is too large, remove its column; if too small, remove its row.
240.approach: At the top-right candidate, a value above target rules out the entire remaining column, while a value below target rules out the entire remaining row. This is staircase elimination, not flattened binary search.

153.title: Find Minimum in Rotated Sorted Array
153.prompt: Find the minimum in a rotated strictly increasing array.
hints: Compare the midpoint with the right endpoint.
If midpoint is larger, the rotation minimum must lie strictly to its right.
153.approach: When nums[mid] exceeds nums[right], the minimum lies in (mid,right]. Otherwise mid is in the final sorted region and can itself be the minimum, so retain it as right.
153.cost: O(log n) time and O(1) space; distinct values are essential to this exact elimination rule.

162.title: Find Peak Element
162.prompt: Find any index strictly larger than its neighbors; adjacent values differ and virtual outside values are negative infinity.
hints: A rising slope guarantees a peak somewhere to its right.
Compare mid with mid+1 and keep the uphill side.
162.approach: If the sequence rises at mid, following it rightward either turns downward at a peak or reaches the right boundary peak. A falling slope gives the symmetric left-side guarantee.
162.cost: O(log n) time and O(1) space. The array need not be globally sorted; the proof uses a local slope.

69.title: Sqrt(x)
69.prompt: Return floor(sqrt(x)) for a nonnegative integer without using a square-root function.
hints: The condition candidate² <= x is monotone.
Search for the largest true candidate and widen multiplication before squaring.
69.approach: A candidate square at most x is feasible and permits searching larger values. Remember the last feasible candidate while shrinking a closed interval.
69.cost: O(log(x+1)) time and O(1) space. long squaring is safe for nonnegative int candidates.

4.title: Median of Two Sorted Arrays
4.prompt: Find the median of two sorted arrays in logarithmic time; their combined length is positive.
hints: Partition both arrays so the left side contains half the combined elements.
Binary-search the cut in the shorter array until both left maxima are no greater than the opposite right minima.
4.approach: A cut i in the shorter array determines cut j in the other. If a left value is too large, shift that cut left; if the opposite left value is too large, shift it right. A valid partition exposes the middle value(s) directly.
4.cost: O(log(min(m,n)+1)) time and O(1) auxiliary space. Sentinel boundaries support empty arrays; widening the even-case sum avoids overflow.

981.title: Time Based Key Value Store
981.prompt: Store values by key and increasing timestamp; retrieve the value at the largest timestamp no later than a query, or an empty string.
hints: Each key has an already ordered history.
Find the first stored timestamp strictly greater than the query, then step back.
981.approach: Append each update to its key’s history. Upper-bound search separates eligible timestamps from future ones; the last eligible entry is the answer.
981.cost: Expected amortized O(1) set and O(log h) get for h updates of the queried key, excluding string hashing costs; O(N) entries overall. Set timestamps must be increasing.

274.title: H-Index
274.prompt: Find the largest h such that at least h papers have at least h citations each.
hints: Sort citations so the number of papers after each position is known.
At index i, n−i papers meet the threshold if citations[i] >= n−i.
274.approach: Scan sorted citation counts from the smallest upward. The first position meeting citations[i] >= n−i yields the largest feasible remaining-paper count.
274.cost: O(n log n) time; O(log n) typical primitive-sort stack space. Mutates input. Bucketing or binary search over feasible h are alternatives.

228.title: Summary Ranges
228.prompt: Summarize each maximal consecutive run in a sorted distinct integer array.
hints: Keep the first value of a run and extend while the next value is consecutive.
Widen the difference to avoid overflow near int endpoints.
228.approach: Sorted distinct input ensures that a nonconsecutive next value permanently ends the current run. Emit either one number or an inclusive start-to-end range.
228.cost: O(n) time and O(1) auxiliary state excluding output strings, under fixed-width integer formatting.

252.title: Meeting Rooms
252.prompt: Determine whether a person can attend every meeting; a meeting ending when another starts does not conflict.
hints: Sort meetings by starting time.
An overlap with the preceding meeting is enough to reject the schedule.
252.approach: In start order, if every meeting begins at or after the previous one ends, all meetings are disjoint. Otherwise the conflicting adjacent pair proves attendance is impossible.
252.cost: O(n log n) time and O(n) object-sort workspace; input order changes.

253.title: Meeting Rooms II
253.prompt: Find the minimum meeting rooms needed for half-open time intervals [start,end).
hints: The answer is the maximum number of simultaneously active meetings.
Add one at each start and subtract one at each end, combining equal-time events.
253.approach: Sweep ordered event deltas. At any time, active meetings need distinct rooms; reusing rooms as meetings end achieves that maximum overlap count.
253.cost: O(n log n) time and O(n) space. Equal-time endings free rooms for starts; a min-heap of end times is another formulation.

452.title: Minimum Number of Arrows to Burst Balloons
452.prompt: Shoot the fewest vertical arrows to intersect every closed horizontal balloon interval.
hints: An arrow can cover every interval containing its coordinate.
Choose the earliest ending uncovered balloon’s endpoint.
452.approach: An arrow at the earliest end covers that balloon and cannot reduce coverage compared with an earlier arrow needed for it. Skip intervals containing the current arrow; start a new arrow after a gap.
452.cost: O(n log n) time and O(n) object-sort workspace; touching closed intervals can share an arrow. Mutates array order.

1851.title: Minimum Interval to Include Each Query
1851.prompt: For each query, find the length of the shortest closed interval containing it, or -1.
hints: Answer queries in sorted order but remember their original positions.
Add intervals whose starts are reached and use a length-ordered heap, discarding expired roots.
1851.approach: When processing query q, insert every interval starting at or before q. Remove heap roots ending before q. The remaining smallest-length root is the shortest eligible interval; expired non-root entries can wait until they reach the top.
1851.cost: O(n log n + q log q + (n+q) log(n+1)) time, O(n+q) space. Interval lengths fit int under the original bounds; interval order is mutated.

2.title: Add Two Numbers
2.prompt: Add two nonnegative integers stored least-significant digit first in linked lists; return a new digit list.
hints: Process the same digit position from both lists together.
Carry survives even after both lists end.
2.approach: At each position, sum available digits and the incoming carry. Emit sum%10 and carry sum/10 to the next position, allocating a separate output list.
2.cost: O(max(m,n)) time and O(max(m,n)) output space; O(1) auxiliary state.

24.title: Swap Nodes in Pairs
24.prompt: Swap each adjacent pair of list nodes by changing links, not their values.
hints: Use a dummy predecessor so swapping the head is not special.
Reconnect predecessor, second, first, and untouched suffix in that order.
24.approach: At each step, before precedes two nodes a,b. Relink them as before→b→a→suffix, then move before to a, the end of the processed pair.
24.cost: O(n) time and O(1) extra space. An unmatched last node stays in place.

25.title: Reverse Nodes in k-Group
25.prompt: Reverse consecutive groups of k linked-list nodes; leave a final short group unchanged.
hints: Confirm that the next group has k nodes before rewiring.
Reverse up to the saved node immediately after that group.
25.approach: Find the kth node from the group predecessor. If it exists, save the suffix and reverse exactly that group toward the suffix; reconnect the predecessor and advance to the old group head.
25.cost: O(n) time and O(1) extra space. Assumes k>=1; nodes are reused.

92.title: Reverse Linked List II
92.prompt: Reverse list positions left through right, using 1-based inclusive positions.
hints: Find the node immediately before the reversed segment.
Repeatedly remove the node after the segment tail and insert it at the segment front.
92.approach: The original segment head becomes its eventual tail. Each front insertion grows the reversed prefix by one while leaving the rest reachable.
92.cost: O(n) time and O(1) space. Input positions are valid; links are changed in place.

61.title: Rotate List
61.prompt: Rotate a list right by k positions without allocating replacement nodes.
hints: Determine the list length and normalize k.
Temporarily connect the tail to the head, then break the cycle at the new tail.
61.approach: A right rotation by k makes position n−k the new head in zero-based terms. Closing the list into a ring lets the suffix reconnect to the original prefix with one cut.
61.cost: O(n) time and O(1) space. The temporary cycle is always broken before returning.

82.title: Remove Duplicates from Sorted List II
82.prompt: In a sorted list, remove every value that appears more than once, retaining only values that occur exactly once.
hints: This task removes all nodes in a duplicate run, not all but one.
Keep a predecessor outside the run while advancing to its end.
82.approach: Sorted order makes duplicates contiguous. Detect a run, skip every node with that value, and link the last confirmed unique predecessor to the next candidate.
82.cost: O(n) time and O(1) auxiliary space.

86.title: Partition List
86.prompt: Stably partition a list so all values below x precede all values at least x.
hints: Build two chains while preserving order inside each.
Terminate the high chain before connecting the low chain to it.
86.approach: Append each node to a low or high tail. These chains preserve encounter order; concatenating them satisfies both the partition and stability requirements.
86.cost: O(n) time and O(1) extra space; reuses nodes and changes links.

160.title: Intersection of Two Linked Lists
160.prompt: Return the node where two acyclic lists begin sharing nodes, or null if they do not intersect.
hints: Equal values are not evidence of a shared node.
Let each pointer traverse both lists, switching heads after null.
160.approach: Traversing A then B and B then A equalizes total traveled lengths. After the differing private prefixes are balanced, the pointers reach the shared suffix together, or both reach null.
160.cost: O(m+n) time and O(1) space; compares node identity and does not mutate input.

142.title: Linked List Cycle II
142.prompt: Return the first node of a cycle in a linked list, or null if acyclic.
hints: First use fast and slow pointers to obtain a meeting inside the cycle.
Reset one pointer to head, then move both at speed one.
142.approach: At the first meeting, the traveled-distance difference is a multiple of the cycle length. This implies that moving one pointer from head and the other from the meeting point at equal speed makes them meet at the cycle entrance.
142.cost: O(n) time for n distinct reachable nodes and O(1) space.

234.title: Palindrome Linked List
234.prompt: Check whether list values form a palindrome using constant extra space.
hints: Find the midpoint and reverse the second half.
Compare the halves, then restore the original links before returning.
234.approach: With the first half ending at slow, reverse slow.next and compare it against the first half. Only the shorter second half needs checking. Reversing again restores the input even after a mismatch.
234.cost: O(n) time and O(1) extra space. Temporarily mutates the second half and restores it.

143.title: Reorder List
143.prompt: Reorder nodes as first, last, second, second-last, and so on without changing values.
hints: Split at the midpoint and reverse the second half.
Weave the two lists, saving both next pointers before changing links.
143.approach: Reversing the second half puts suffix nodes in the needed order. Alternately taking one node from each half produces the desired weave; the first half has at least as many nodes.
143.cost: O(n) time and O(1) extra space; mutates list links.

148.title: Sort List
148.prompt: Sort a linked list in ascending order in O(n log n) time.
hints: Merge sort does not require array-style random access.
Split with fast/slow pointers, recursively sort each half, and merge their nodes.
148.approach: Cut before the midpoint so each recursive call gets a smaller list. Merge two sorted results by always attaching the smaller head.
148.cost: O(n log n) time and O(log n) recursive stack space; reuses nodes. Bottom-up merge sort can eliminate the recursion stack.

138.title: Copy List with Random Pointer
138.prompt: Deep-copy a list whose nodes have next and random pointers; random points anywhere in the list or to null.
138.example: A.random=B, B.random=A → copied nodes with the same relationships and no links to originals.
hints: Create one copied node for each original node before assigning random links.
Use an original-node → copied-node map to translate both pointer types.
138.approach: The first pass establishes a bijection from originals to clones. The second pass uses that map to recreate every edge, including backward random pointers and null references.
138.cost: Expected O(n) time and O(n) auxiliary map space, plus O(n) copied nodes. The original list is unchanged.
138.supportCode: class Node { int val; Node next, random; Node(int val) { this.val = val; } }

146.title: LRU Cache
146.prompt: Implement a fixed-capacity cache where get and put update recency and the least recently used key is evicted when full.
146.example: capacity=2; put(1,1), put(2,2), get(1), put(3,3) → key 2 evicted
hints: A map finds entries; a doubly linked list updates recency in constant time.
Use sentinel head and tail nodes to simplify moving and evicting entries.
146.approach: The list runs from most to least recent. Map lookup finds a node, unlink/reinsert moves it to the front, and eviction removes tail.prev from both structures.
146.cost: Expected O(1) get and put; O(capacity) storage. Updating an existing key also makes it most recent.

202.title: Happy Number
202.prompt: Determine whether repeatedly replacing a positive integer by the sum of squared decimal digits eventually reaches 1.
hints: Repeated states form a deterministic cycle if 1 is never reached.
Use Floyd’s fast/slow method on the digit-square transformation.
202.approach: The transformation quickly enters a finite bounded state set. Slow advances once, fast twice; a meeting at 1 means success, while a meeting elsewhere identifies a non-1 cycle.
202.cost: O(log n) digit work to enter a small bounded range, then bounded cycle work for Java int; O(1) space.

71.title: Simplify Path
71.prompt: Normalize an absolute Unix-style path: ignore empty components and dot, and let dot-dot move to the parent when possible.
hints: Path components are unfinished directory choices.
Push normal names; pop one name for dot-dot.
71.approach: A deque stores the canonical directory sequence. Empty components and dot have no effect; dot-dot removes the latest directory without moving above root.
71.cost: O(n) time and O(n) space including split components and output. Names such as ... are ordinary directory names.

394.title: Decode String
394.prompt: Decode nested repetition expressions of the form count[substring], with positive counts and valid syntax.
hints: Each opening bracket pauses the current output and repeat count.
On closing, append the completed nested text to its saved parent the required number of times.
394.approach: Two stacks store parent builders and repetition counts. A closing bracket completes one nested scope, restoring the parent and extending it with the repeated child.
394.cost: O(n+dL) upper-bound time for input length n, nesting depth d, and decoded length L, because nested text may be recopied at each level. O(n+L) peak space.

224.title: Basic Calculator
224.prompt: Evaluate a valid expression with integers, plus, minus, parentheses, and spaces; unary minus is allowed.
hints: Keep the accumulated result and the sign of the next term within each scope.
Save the outer result and sign on opening a parenthesis.
224.approach: Numbers are immediately added with the current sign. Parentheses begin a fresh local result; closing combines it with the saved outer result using the saved sign.
224.cost: O(n) time and O(d) stack space for nesting depth d. Input validity and integer-result bounds follow the original problem.

32.title: Longest Valid Parentheses
32.prompt: Find the longest contiguous substring of correctly matched parentheses.
hints: Store indices so a match can reveal a length.
Keep a base index just before the current possibly valid region.
32.approach: The stack starts with -1. Push opening indices; on a closing bracket, pop once. An empty stack means an unmatched closer resets the base, otherwise the current valid suffix begins after the remaining top.
32.cost: O(n) time and O(n) space. The sentinel/base represents a boundary, not an opening parenthesis.

853.title: Car Fleet
853.prompt: Count car fleets reaching a target when cars move forward and cannot pass; cars meeting exactly at the target form one fleet.
hints: Process cars from nearest the target to farthest.
Compare each arrival time with the fleet immediately ahead.
853.approach: A trailing car whose solo arrival time is no greater than the fleet ahead will catch it, so it joins that fleet. A larger time starts a new, slower fleet. This is a monotone frontier scan after sorting.
853.cost: O(n log n) time and O(n) ordering-array space; only one frontier time is needed after sorting.

918.title: Maximum Sum Circular Subarray
918.prompt: Find the maximum sum of a nonempty circular subarray, using each position at most once.
hints: Duplicate the array so every circular subarray becomes an ordinary range of length at most n.
Use increasing prefix sums in a deque to obtain the smallest eligible starting prefix.
918.approach: For each end boundary, maximize currentPrefix−minimumEarlierPrefix among starts at most n positions behind it. Expire old indices at the front and remove dominated larger prefix sums at the back.
918.cost: O(n) time and O(n) space; each prefix enters/leaves once. Query-before-insert forbids empty ranges. A maximum/minimum Kadane formulation can reduce space to O(1).

226.title: Invert Binary Tree
226.prompt: Mirror a binary tree by exchanging left and right children at every node.
hints: Each child subtree must also be mirrored.
Save one child before exchanging recursive results.
226.approach: Recursively mirror both original subtrees, then assign them to opposite sides. Null subtrees remain null.
226.cost: O(n) time and O(h) call-stack space; mutates tree links.

100.title: Same Tree
100.prompt: Determine whether two trees have identical structure and corresponding values.
hints: Null positions are part of the structure.
Require equal roots and recursively equal left and right pairs.
100.approach: If either node is null, equality requires both null. Otherwise value equality and both corresponding subtree equalities are necessary and sufficient.
100.cost: O(min(n,m)) visited-node comparisons up to early mismatch, O(h) recursion space bounded by the compared depth.

101.title: Symmetric Tree
101.prompt: Check whether a binary tree is symmetric around its center.
hints: Compare mirrored positions, not matching left positions.
Pair left.left with right.right and left.right with right.left.
101.approach: A mirrored pair must have equal root values and crosswise mirrored children. Null positions must match as well.
101.cost: O(n) time and O(h) recursive space.

110.title: Balanced Binary Tree
110.prompt: Determine whether every tree node has left/right subtree heights differing by at most one.
hints: Recomputing height at every node repeats work.
Return height when balanced and a failure sentinel otherwise.
110.approach: One postorder traversal combines heights. A -1 result propagates an unbalanced subtree immediately; otherwise the helper returns its ordinary height.
110.cost: O(n) time and O(h) stack space; each subtree height is computed once.

572.title: Subtree of Another Tree
572.prompt: Determine whether subRoot matches a complete subtree of root, including structure and values.
hints: Every node of the larger tree is a possible matching root.
A candidate must match both values and null structure exactly.
572.approach: Test structural equality at the current node, then recursively try each child as a new candidate root. An empty target is treated as matching for a general helper contract.
572.cost: O(nm) worst-case time for tree sizes n and m; O(hRoot+hSub) upper-bound recursion space. Repeated values can force many nearly complete comparisons.

112.title: Path Sum
112.prompt: Decide whether any root-to-leaf path sums to targetSum.
hints: Subtract each visited value from the remaining target.
Success requires a leaf, not merely an internal prefix with the right sum.
112.approach: Each recursive call asks whether its subtree has a path supplying the remaining sum. A leaf succeeds exactly when its value equals that remainder.
112.cost: O(n) time and O(h) stack space. Path sums fit int under the original limits.

129.title: Sum Root to Leaf Numbers
129.prompt: Each node is a decimal digit. Sum the numbers represented by all root-to-leaf paths.
hints: Carry the current numeric prefix downward.
Append a digit with prefix*10+digit; count it only at a leaf.
129.approach: Each branch receives its own numeric prefix by value. Internal nodes sum their child results; leaves contribute exactly one complete path number.
129.cost: O(n) time and O(h) space. Values and final result fit int under the problem constraints.

1448.title: Count Good Nodes In Binary Tree
1448.prompt: Count nodes whose value is at least every value on the path from the root to that node.
hints: Only the largest ancestor value matters.
Pass that maximum down independently along each branch.
1448.approach: A node is good exactly when its value reaches the inherited maximum. Update the maximum for children; sibling branches do not share mutable path state.
1448.cost: O(n) time and O(h) stack space.

124.title: Binary Tree Maximum Path Sum
124.prompt: Find the largest sum along any nonempty simple path in a binary tree; the path need not include the root.
hints: The answer may join left and right branches at one node.
Return only one extendable branch to the parent, and ignore negative child gains.
124.approach: At each node, test node.val plus both nonnegative child gains as a complete path. Return node.val plus the larger single gain so the parent never creates a forked path.
124.cost: O(n) time and O(h) space. Initialize best below every node value so all-negative trees still return a nonempty path.

437.title: Path Sum III
437.prompt: Count downward ancestor-to-descendant paths with a target sum; paths may start and stop anywhere.
hints: A downward path sum is a difference between two root-path prefix sums.
Keep only prefix counts on the current recursion path and undo the current prefix when returning.
437.approach: Before visiting a node, the frequency map contains ancestor boundaries only. The number of matching paths ending here is count(prefix−target). Adding before children and removing afterward isolates sibling histories.
437.cost: Expected O(n) time and O(h) map/stack space. long prefixes prevent overflow along long paths; answer fits original bounds.

94.title: Binary Tree Inorder Traversal
94.prompt: Return a binary tree’s values in left-root-right order.
hints: A stack remembers nodes whose left subtree is being explored.
Descend left, visit the popped node, then enter its right subtree.
94.approach: The stack simulates recursive inorder traversal without using Java call frames. Every node is pushed once and visited once.
94.cost: O(n) time and O(h) auxiliary stack space, plus O(n) output.

105.title: Construct Binary Tree from Preorder and Inorder Traversal
105.prompt: Reconstruct a binary tree from preorder and inorder traversals containing distinct values.
105.example: pre=[3,9,20,15,7], in=[9,3,15,20,7] → root 3 with left 9 and right 20
hints: Preorder supplies the next subtree root.
Its inorder position separates left and right subtree ranges.
105.approach: Consume preorder roots in sequence while recursively restricting inorder boundaries. A value-to-inorder-index map finds each split without rescanning.
105.cost: Expected O(n) time; O(n) map and O(h) stack space, plus output nodes. Assumes consistent traversals with distinct values.

106.title: Construct Binary Tree from Inorder and Postorder Traversal
106.prompt: Reconstruct a binary tree from inorder and postorder traversals with distinct values.
hints: The last remaining postorder value is the subtree root.
When consuming postorder backward, build the right subtree before the left.
106.approach: Reverse postorder visits root, right, left. The inorder map splits the range; building in that reversed order aligns every next consumed value with its subtree.
106.cost: Expected O(n) time and O(n+h) auxiliary space, plus output nodes.

114.title: Flatten Binary Tree to Linked List
114.prompt: Flatten a binary tree in place into a right-linked chain in preorder; every left pointer must become null.
hints: Preorder tells you the next node to append.
Save children on a stack before overwriting the previous node’s links.
114.approach: Process a preorder stack, pushing right before left. Link the previous node to the current node and clear its left child, preserving the remaining frontier in the stack.
114.cost: O(n) time and O(h) explicit stack space. Mutates the tree; the algorithm does not allocate replacement nodes.

297.title: Serialize And Deserialize Binary Tree
297.prompt: Serialize a binary tree to text and reconstruct its exact values and null structure.
hints: Values alone do not determine shape.
Use preorder with an explicit marker for every missing child.
297.approach: Preorder emits a value followed by two subtree encodings; # represents null. The decoder consumes exactly one token for each root and recursively consumes its two children, making the grammar unambiguous.
297.cost: O(n) time and O(n) serialized/token space for fixed-width values; O(h) recursion depth. Decoder assumes output from this serializer.

222.title: Count Complete Tree Nodes
222.prompt: Count nodes in a complete binary tree faster than a full traversal.
hints: A complete subtree whose far-left and far-right heights agree is perfect.
Count a perfect subtree with 2^height−1 instead of visiting its nodes.
222.approach: Measure both edge heights. Equality proves fullness under the completeness guarantee; otherwise recurse, with one child guaranteed perfect at each level.
222.cost: O(log² n) time and O(log n) recursive space for complete trees. The perfect-subtree shortcut is not valid for arbitrary trees.

103.title: Binary Tree Zigzag Level Order Traversal
103.prompt: Return tree levels alternating left-to-right and right-to-left value order.
hints: Keep ordinary BFS traversal but change where each level value is inserted.
Append values on one level and prepend on the next.
103.approach: The queue still discovers children left-to-right. A per-level deque reverses only the presentation order, keeping traversal logic independent of zigzag output.
103.cost: O(n) time; O(w) frontier space plus O(n) output.

637.title: Average of Levels in Binary Tree
637.prompt: Return the arithmetic mean of values at each tree depth.
hints: Use a fixed queue size to isolate a level.
Accumulate into a wide numeric type before dividing.
637.approach: BFS separates levels. Sum each fixed-size layer using long and divide by its node count in floating point.
637.cost: O(n) time and O(w) queue space, plus O(h) output.

117.title: Populating Next Right Pointers in Each Node II
117.prompt: Set each tree node’s next pointer to its neighbor on the same level, or null at the level end.
hints: Use fixed-size BFS layers.
Connect each removed node to the next node removed in that layer.
117.approach: A previous pointer inside the current layer links adjacent nodes. Explicitly set the final node’s next to null so preexisting next values cannot leak across levels.
117.cost: O(n) time and O(w) queue space. A level-link traversal with a dummy next-level head can reduce extra space to O(1).
117.supportCode: class Node { int val; Node left, right, next; Node(int val) { this.val = val; } }

108.title: Convert Sorted Array to Binary Search Tree
108.prompt: Build a height-balanced BST from a sorted distinct integer array.
hints: The middle value splits the ordered values into balanced halves.
Recursively build left and right index ranges without slicing arrays.
108.approach: Selecting each range midpoint keeps subtree sizes within one, while sorted ranges ensure every left value is smaller and every right value larger.
108.cost: O(n) time and O(log n) recursive space, plus O(n) output nodes.

530.title: Minimum Absolute Difference in BST
530.prompt: Find the minimum absolute difference between values of two different BST nodes.
hints: In sorted order, a closest pair must be adjacent.
Use inorder traversal and compare each visited value with the preceding value.
530.approach: Inorder emits sorted values; any gap spanning intervening values is no smaller than an adjacent gap. Only the previous value is needed.
530.cost: O(n) time and O(h) space. At least two nodes and the original bounded nonnegative values are assumed.

173.title: Binary Search Tree Iterator
173.prompt: Implement a BST iterator returning values in ascending order through next() and hasNext().
hints: Keep the path to the next inorder node on a stack.
After popping a node, push the left spine of its right subtree.
173.approach: The stack contains pending inorder ancestors. Each node is pushed and popped once across the iterator’s lifetime, so a costly descent is amortized over later calls.
173.cost: O(h) initialization/storage; amortized O(1) next over a full traversal, O(h) worst case for one call; O(1) hasNext. next requires an available element.

427.title: Construct Quad Tree
427.prompt: Represent a binary square grid of power-of-two size as a quad tree; uniform regions become leaves.
hints: A region is a leaf exactly when every cell matches its first cell.
Otherwise split into four equally sized quadrants.
427.approach: Recursively test uniformity, then build top-left, top-right, bottom-left, and bottom-right children for mixed regions. Internal node values are arbitrary; only leaf values encode cells.
427.cost: O(n² log n) worst-case time for repeated region scans, O(log n) recursion space plus up to O(n²) output. Prefix sums can make each uniformity test constant-time.
427.supportCode: class Node { boolean val, isLeaf; Node topLeft, topRight, bottomLeft, bottomRight; Node(boolean val, boolean isLeaf) { this.val=val; this.isLeaf=isLeaf; } }

133.title: Clone Graph
133.prompt: Deep-copy every node and edge reachable from an undirected graph node, including cycles.
133.example: Two nodes linked to each other → two new nodes linked to each other
hints: Record a clone before traversing its neighbors.
A map from original nodes to clones prevents cycles from causing repeated copying.
133.approach: Create the current clone and memoize it immediately. Recursive neighbor calls reuse existing clones, so shared neighbors and back edges retain their structure.
133.cost: Expected O(V+E) time and O(V) map/recursion space, plus cloned graph output. Deep graphs may require iterative traversal.
133.supportCode: class Node { int val; List<Node> neighbors = new ArrayList<>(); Node(int val) { this.val = val; } }

130.title: Surrounded Regions
130.prompt: Capture O regions completely enclosed by X in a board; border-connected O cells remain unchanged.
130.example: An isolated interior O becomes X; an O connected to the border stays O.
hints: It is easier to identify cells that cannot be captured.
Flood all border O cells, then flip the remaining unmarked O cells.
130.approach: Mark every O reachable from the boundary with a temporary symbol. These are exactly the safe regions. A final pass captures unmarked O and restores safe cells.
130.cost: O(RC) time and O(RC) worst-case call-stack space. Mutates the board; use an explicit frontier when recursion depth is unsafe.

695.title: Max Area of Island
695.prompt: Return the number of cells in the largest four-directionally connected island of ones.
hints: Each new component needs a size, not just a visited mark.
A flood call returns one plus the sizes of newly discovered neighbors.
695.approach: Flood each unvisited land component, setting visited cells to zero. Sum each component’s cells and keep the maximum.
695.cost: O(RC) time and O(RC) worst-case recursive space. Mutates the grid; iterative flood fill avoids Java call-stack limits.

417.title: Pacific Atlantic Water Flow
417.prompt: Find cells from which water can flow downhill or level to both the top/left ocean and bottom/right ocean.
hints: Searching from every cell repeats work.
Reverse the flow: flood uphill from each ocean border, then intersect reachable sets.
417.approach: A reverse edge goes to a neighbor at least as high. Reaching a cell from an ocean in this reverse graph proves an original downhill route to that ocean.
417.cost: O(RC) time and O(RC) space including visitation and worst-case recursion. Reverse searches do not mutate heights.

286.title: Walls And Gates
286.prompt: Fill each empty room with its distance to the nearest gate, respecting walls. Gates are 0, walls -1, empty rooms Integer.MAX_VALUE.
hints: All gates have distance zero simultaneously.
Start one BFS with every gate and claim each empty room on first discovery.
286.approach: Multi-source BFS visits rooms in increasing distance from the nearest gate. The first discovery fixes the shortest distance because all moves cost one.
286.cost: O(RC) time and O(RC) queue space. Updates rooms in place; unreachable rooms retain INF.

127.title: Word Ladder
127.prompt: Find the number of words in a shortest one-letter transformation from beginWord to endWord, using dictionary words for all intermediate steps.
hints: Words are vertices and one-character substitutions are edges.
Use BFS and remove words from the unvisited dictionary when enqueuing.
127.approach: Each BFS layer adds one transformation. Generate neighbors by replacing every character with each lowercase letter; the first arrival at endWord has minimum length.
127.cost: Expected O(N·26·L²) time including length-L string copying/hashing, O(NL) stored-word/frontier space; N dictionary words of common length L.

433.title: Minimum Genetic Mutation
433.prompt: Find the fewest one-character gene mutations from startGene to endGene; every new gene must appear in the bank.
433.example: AACCGGTT → AACCGGTA with that gene in bank → 1
hints: This is shortest path in an unweighted graph of valid genes.
Generate substitutions from A,C,G,T and use BFS.
433.approach: BFS explores increasing mutation counts. Remove a bank entry when enqueued so each gene is visited once; equal start and end requires zero mutations.
433.cost: Expected O(BL²) time and O(BL) space for bank size B and gene length L, with alphabet size 4; the original L=8 is fixed.

909.title: Snakes and Ladders
909.prompt: Find the fewest die rolls to reach the last square on a boustrophedon-numbered board with snakes and ladders. Apply at most one transport per roll.
hints: Treat each landing outcome after one die roll as an edge.
Convert square numbers into alternating-direction rows measured upward from the bottom.
909.approach: BFS over square labels explores roll counts. Map each raw landing square to a board cell, take its single snake/ladder if present, then mark the resulting square visited.
909.cost: O(n²) time and space since each square has at most six roll outcomes.

399.title: Evaluate Division
399.prompt: Given consistent equations a/b=value, answer division queries through known variables, or -1.0 when no relationship is known.
hints: Equations form a weighted graph with reciprocal reverse edges.
Multiply weights along any known path between the query variables.
399.approach: Build edges a→b with value and b→a with its reciprocal. DFS carries the cumulative ratio. Consistency guarantees all valid paths give the same ratio; this is multiplicative reachability, not a shortest-path optimization.
399.cost: Expected O(E+Q(V+E)) time and O(V+E) graph/traversal space, excluding output and variable-string hashing costs.

323.title: Number of Connected Components In An Undirected Graph
323.prompt: Count connected components in an undirected graph with n labeled vertices, including isolated ones.
hints: Start with n separate components.
Only a successful merge reduces the component count.
323.approach: Union endpoints of every edge. Equal roots mean the edge adds no new connectivity; different roots merge two previously separate groups.
323.cost: O(n+E α(n)) amortized time and O(n) space using union by size and path compression.

261.title: Graph Valid Tree
261.prompt: Determine whether n vertices and undirected edges form exactly one tree.
hints: A tree on n vertices needs exactly n−1 edges.
With that edge count, rejecting every cycle is enough to establish connectivity too.
261.approach: Check the edge count, then union endpoints. A failed union reveals a cycle. If all n−1 unions succeed, exactly one component remains.
261.cost: O(n+E α(n)) amortized time and O(n) space. Assumes n>=1.

269.title: Alien Dictionary
269.prompt: Infer a valid ordering of lowercase alien letters from a sorted word list, or return empty when the list is inconsistent.
hints: Only the first differing character in adjacent words establishes an order edge.
Reject a longer word placed before its own prefix, and topologically sort distinct edges.
269.approach: Collect every present letter, then add one dependency at the first difference of each adjacent word pair. Kahn’s algorithm returns an order if no cycle exists. Sets prevent duplicate edges from inflating indegrees.
269.cost: O(L+V+E) time and O(V+E) persistent space for total input characters L. toCharArray creates up to one word-length temporary allocation; alphabet has at most 26 letters.

329.title: Longest Increasing Path In a Matrix
329.prompt: Find the longest strictly increasing four-directional path in a matrix.
hints: Strictly increasing moves cannot form a directed cycle.
Memoize the longest path starting at each cell.
329.approach: Each state is one cell. Its answer is one plus the best answer of a strictly larger neighbor, or one if none exists. Strict growth supplies a DAG, so recursion needs no path-visited set.
329.cost: O(RC) time and O(RC) memo/stack space. A topological-layer implementation avoids deep recursion on long increasing paths.

332.title: Reconstruct Itinerary
332.prompt: Use every airline ticket exactly once to form the lexicographically smallest valid itinerary starting at JFK; a complete itinerary is guaranteed.
hints: Choosing the smallest outgoing ticket as a final route step can strand unused edges.
Use lexical edge selection inside an Euler-trail traversal, appending airports only when their outgoing edges are exhausted.
332.approach: Hierholzer’s algorithm consumes each directed edge once. A min-heap chooses outgoing destinations lexically; dead ends are prepended during unwinding, which delays terminal branches until their proper place in the completed Euler trail.
332.cost: O(E log(E+1)) time and O(E) space for fixed-length airport codes. This is an Euler-trail extension, not ordinary node-visited DFS.

778.title: Swim In Rising Water
778.prompt: On a square elevation grid, find the earliest water level allowing a four-directional path from top-left to bottom-right.
hints: A path’s required time is its highest elevation.
Relax neighbors using max(currentTime, neighborHeight), and extract the smallest time first.
778.approach: Dijkstra’s bottleneck variant keeps the minimum possible maximum elevation to each cell. Extending a path never lowers its requirement, so the smallest current extraction is safe.
778.cost: O(n² log(n²)) time and O(n²) space. Binary search on water level plus reachability is an alternative.

787.title: Cheapest Flights Within K Stops
787.prompt: Find the cheapest directed flight route with at most k intermediate stops, or -1 if impossible.
hints: At most k stops means at most k+1 edges.
Each relaxation round must read the previous round, not its own updates.
787.approach: Bounded Bellman–Ford stores minimum cost using at most a given number of edges. Copy the distance array each round, then relax from the old array so one round adds at most one flight.
787.cost: O((k+1)(V+E)) time, including array copies; O(V) extra space. Sentinel arithmetic is safe under original bounds. Ordinary one-distance-per-node Dijkstra loses the stop constraint.

1584.title: Min Cost to Connect All Points
1584.prompt: Connect all points with minimum total Manhattan edge length.
hints: The objective is one minimum spanning tree, not shortest paths from a source.
Repeatedly add the unconnected point with the cheapest edge into the growing tree.
1584.approach: Dense Prim’s algorithm tracks each outside point’s cheapest edge to the current tree. The minimum crossing edge is safe by the cut property. Compute Manhattan weights on demand rather than storing every pair.
1584.cost: O(n²) time and O(n) auxiliary space. Coordinates and result fit int under original bounds. Kruskal with DSU is an alternative but explicitly sorting all pairwise edges costs more space.

215.title: Kth Largest Element in an Array
215.prompt: Find the kth largest array value, counting duplicate occurrences separately.
hints: Keep only the largest k values seen so far.
The smallest retained value is the kth largest once the scan completes.
215.approach: Insert each value into a min-heap and remove the smallest whenever its size exceeds k. The retained multiset consists of the k largest processed occurrences.
215.cost: O(n log(k+1)) time and O(k) space. Randomized quickselect is an expected O(n)-time alternative that mutates input.

703.title: Kth Largest Element In a Stream
703.prompt: Maintain the kth largest value as integers arrive in a stream.
hints: Only the largest k occurrences affect future answers.
Use a min-heap capped at k entries across constructor and add calls.
703.approach: The bounded heap invariant persists between operations. Once at least k values have arrived, its root is the kth largest occurrence.
703.cost: O(log(k+1)) per add and O(k) space; O(n log(k+1)) initialization. Queries are guaranteed to have at least k total values.

1046.title: Last Stone Weight
1046.prompt: Repeatedly smash the two heaviest stones; equal weights disappear, otherwise reinsert their difference. Return the final weight or zero.
hints: The next operation always needs the two largest current values.
Use a max-heap and reinsert only a positive difference.
1046.approach: A max-heap directly models the repeated selection rule. Each smash reduces the number of stones by at least one, so there are at most n−1 rounds.
1046.cost: O(n log n) time and O(n) space.

973.title: K Closest Points to Origin
973.prompt: Return k points with smallest Euclidean distance to the origin; output order is arbitrary.
hints: Squared distance preserves ordering without square roots.
Keep a size-k max-heap so the farthest retained point is evicted first.
973.approach: The heap contains the k closest points processed so far. A new point competes with the current farthest retained point; duplicates remain separate input occurrences.
973.cost: O(n log(k+1)) time and O(k) heap/output-reference space. Returned point arrays are shared with input.

373.title: Find K Pairs with Smallest Sums
373.prompt: Return up to k pairs with smallest sums, taking one value from each of two sorted arrays.
hints: For a fixed first-array index, pairing with the second array forms a sorted sequence.
Merge these row sequences with a heap holding one frontier pair per row.
373.approach: Seed the first pair from at most k rows. Pop the smallest sum and advance only its second-array index. Later rows cannot be required ahead of k no-larger first pairs, except interchangeable ties.
373.cost: O((h+z) log(h+1)) time for h=min(k,m) seeded rows and z emitted pairs; O(h) heap space plus O(z) output.

502.title: IPO
502.prompt: Choose at most k distinct projects to maximize capital; a project is available when its required capital is at most current capital, and its nonnegative profit is added.
hints: Available projects change as capital grows.
Sort by required capital, then select the highest profit among unlocked projects.
502.approach: Unlock every project currently affordable and place profits in a max-heap. The largest available nonnegative profit leaves at least as much capital for all later choices as any other available project.
502.cost: O(n log n + min(k,n) log(n+1)) time and O(n) space. Capital is an eligibility threshold, not a cost subtracted on selection; final capital fits int by the problem guarantee.

621.title: Task Scheduler
621.prompt: Schedule uppercase unit-time tasks with at least n intervening intervals between equal letters; minimize total intervals including idle time.
621.example: AAABBB, n=2 → 8 via A B idle A B idle A B
hints: The most frequent tasks force separated frames.
Compare the forced-frame length with the total task count.
621.approach: If maxFrequency=f and ties letters attain f, placing their first f−1 occurrences forces (f−1) frames of length n+1, followed by ties final tasks. Other letters fill gaps; if there are enough, total task count dominates.
621.cost: O(T+26) time and O(1) space for the fixed alphabet. This computes only length; a heap plus cooldown queue can construct a schedule.

355.title: Design Twitter
355.prompt: Implement tweet posting, following/unfollowing, and a news feed of the ten most recent tweets by the user or followed users.
hints: Each author’s tweets form a time-sorted stream.
Merge one newest frontier tweet per relevant author using a max-heap.
355.approach: Store append-only tweet histories and follow sets. For a feed, seed each author’s latest tweet, repeatedly take the newest, and advance backward in only that author’s history until ten items are collected.
355.cost: Expected amortized O(1) post/follow/unfollow; O((F+10) log(F+1)) feed time and O(F) feed workspace for F relevant authors. Persistent storage is O(tweets+follow relationships). int timestamps suffice for the original operation bound.

17.title: Letter Combinations of a Phone Number
17.prompt: Return all letter strings represented by phone digits 2 through 9; an empty input yields no strings.
hints: Each digit adds one level of choices.
Append one mapped letter, recurse to the next digit, then remove it.
17.approach: The recursive depth is the next digit index, so each completed path chooses exactly one letter per digit and each possible string has one construction path.
17.cost: O(d·4^d) worst-case time/output size and O(d) recursion/path space for d digits. The fixed mapping has constant size.

22.title: Generate Parentheses
22.prompt: Generate every valid string containing n matched pairs of parentheses.
hints: Never close more parentheses than have opened.
Add an opener while open<n and a closer while close<open.
22.approach: A prefix is extendable exactly when it has at most n openings and no more closings than openings. Restricting choices to those conditions produces only valid completed strings.
22.cost: O(n Cn) time and output size for Catalan number Cn, O(n) auxiliary path/stack space.

40.title: Combination Sum II
40.prompt: Return unique combinations totaling target, using each candidate occurrence at most once; candidates are positive and may repeat.
hints: Sort so equal choices are adjacent and oversized values can stop a loop.
Skip equal choices at the same recursion depth, but permit later copies at deeper levels.
40.approach: Use increasing indices so each occurrence is used at most once. Skipping adjacent equal candidates only when i>start removes duplicate construction branches without forbidding valid repeated-value combinations.
40.cost: O(n·2^n) conservative enumeration/copying bound plus sorting; O(n) auxiliary recursion/path space excluding output. Sorts input.

77.title: Combinations
77.prompt: Return all ways to choose k distinct numbers from 1 through n, ignoring order.
hints: Increasing choices give each combination one construction order.
Stop the loop early if too few numbers remain to fill the path.
77.approach: A recursive start value enforces increasing order. If need choices remain, the next value cannot exceed n−need+1, which prunes incomplete branches.
77.cost: O(k·C(n,k)) output-sensitive time for k>=1; O(k) auxiliary space and O(k·C(n,k)) output.

90.title: Subsets II
90.prompt: Return all distinct subsets of an integer array that may contain duplicates.
hints: Sort values so equivalent choices are adjacent.
Skip equal candidates only at the same depth, not throughout a path.
90.approach: Each recursion records its current subset. Increasing indices avoid reorderings; same-depth duplicate skipping avoids starting equivalent branches while still permitting multiple copies.
90.cost: O(n·2^n) worst-case time/output and O(n) auxiliary recursion/path space. Sorts the input.

131.title: Palindrome Partitioning
131.prompt: Partition a string into every possible sequence of palindromic pieces.
hints: At each start boundary, choose a palindromic next piece.
Precompute palindrome intervals so repeated checks become constant-time.
131.approach: A DP table marks s[left:right] palindromic when endpoints match and its interior is empty, one character, or already palindromic. Backtracking then enumerates valid next cuts until the string is consumed.
131.cost: O(n²+n·2^n) upper-bound time including substring/copy work; O(n²) table plus path/stack, excluding potentially exponential output.

51.title: N-Queens
51.prompt: Place n queens on an n×n board so no pair shares a row, column, or diagonal; return all boards.
hints: Place one queen per row, so only columns and diagonals need checking.
Track row−column and row+column diagonal identities.
51.approach: One row per recursive level prevents row conflicts. Boolean occupancy arrays reject unsafe columns and diagonals in constant time, and each branch restores them after exploring.
51.cost: O(n·n! + S n²) conservative time bound for candidate scanning and S output boards; O(n²) working board plus O(n) recursion/flags, excluding output.

52.title: N-Queens II
52.prompt: Count valid n-queen placements without returning the boards.
hints: The same occupied columns and diagonals reject unsafe choices.
Return one when all rows are filled and sum branch counts.
52.approach: A recursive state fixes the previous rows and their occupied lines. Each safe column creates one disjoint branch; complete placements contribute one to the count.
52.cost: O(n·n!) conservative time bound and O(n) auxiliary arrays/recursion space. Counting avoids materializing boards.

212.title: Word Search II
212.prompt: Find all dictionary words formed by four-directionally adjacent board cells without reusing a cell within one word.
hints: Searching every word independently repeats common prefixes.
Build a trie, follow only existing prefix edges, and restore board cells after each path.
212.approach: Trie nodes represent shared dictionary prefixes. DFS consumes a board letter only when the corresponding child exists; terminal words are emitted once by clearing their stored word, while path-local visitation is undone on return.
212.cost: O(W+RC·4^L) conservative worst-case time for total dictionary length W and maximum word length L; trie pruning usually saves work. O(W+min(L,RC)) auxiliary space plus output; board is restored.

14.title: Longest Common Prefix
14.prompt: Return the longest prefix shared by every string, or empty if none exists.
hints: A common prefix must also be a prefix of the first string.
Compare each character position across all strings and stop at the first disagreement or end.
14.approach: Vertical scanning tests whether every string contains the same character at a position. All earlier positions have already been proved common, so the first failure determines the exact prefix.
14.cost: O(total inspected characters) time, O(1) auxiliary state plus copied output. A trie is useful for repeated prefix queries but unnecessary for this single query.

28.title: Find the Index of the First Occurrence in a String
28.prompt: Return the first starting index of needle in haystack, or -1 if absent.
hints: When a partial match fails, its suffix may already match a shorter pattern prefix.
Precompute the longest proper-prefix/suffix length for each pattern prefix.
28.approach: KMP preserves the length of the matched pattern prefix. On mismatch, fall back through its prefix table instead of restarting the text scan. A full match returns the current index minus pattern length plus one.
28.cost: O(n+m) time and O(m) space. This is a prefix-function string-search extension, not a trie or a conventional sliding-window count algorithm.

5.title: Longest Palindromic Substring
5.prompt: Return any longest contiguous palindromic substring.
hints: Every palindrome has a center at a character or between characters.
Expand both odd and even centers while mirrored characters match.
5.approach: Expanding all centers examines every possible palindrome at its unique center. Record the longest successful interval and return its substring.
5.cost: O(n²) time and O(1) auxiliary state plus output. Interval DP is an O(n²)-space alternative.

647.title: Palindromic Substrings
647.prompt: Count palindromic substring occurrences; identical text at different positions counts separately.
hints: Each successful center expansion corresponds to one occurrence.
Count every matching radius for both odd and even centers.
647.approach: A palindrome occurrence has exactly one center and radius. Counting successful expansions therefore counts every occurrence once without a set.
647.cost: O(n²) time and O(1) space; the count fits int under original length limits.

91.title: Decode Ways
91.prompt: Count decodings of a digit string under 1→A through 26→Z; zero has no standalone decoding.
hints: Classify a decoding by whether its final letter uses one digit or two.
A single digit must be nonzero; a pair must lie in 10 through 26.
91.approach: dp[i] counts decodings of the first i digits. Add dp[i−1] for a valid final digit and dp[i−2] for a valid final pair; the empty prefix has one decoding.
91.cost: O(n) time and O(n) space, reducible to two previous states. The answer is guaranteed to fit int; input is nonempty.

53.title: Maximum Subarray
53.prompt: Find the largest sum of any nonempty contiguous subarray.
hints: Track the best sum ending exactly at the current position.
Either extend the preceding subarray or begin anew at this value.
53.approach: A best subarray ending at i is either nums[i] alone or the best ending at i−1 extended by nums[i]. Keep a separate maximum over all ending positions.
53.cost: O(n) time and O(1) space. Initialize from an element so all-negative arrays still select a nonempty subarray.

152.title: Maximum Product Subarray
152.prompt: Find the largest product of a nonempty contiguous subarray.
hints: A negative value can turn the smallest product into the largest.
Track both minimum and maximum products ending here.
152.approach: Before multiplying by a negative value, swap the best and worst previous products. Each new extreme either starts at the current number or extends the corresponding previous extreme.
152.cost: O(n) time and O(1) space. Products fit int under the original subarray-product bounds; zeros naturally reset extrema.

213.title: House Robber II
213.prompt: Maximize money robbed from circularly arranged houses without taking adjacent houses.
hints: The first and last houses cannot both be taken.
Solve the linear problem excluding the first and excluding the last, then take the better result.
213.approach: Every legal circular selection belongs to at least one of those two cases. Each linear range uses the usual skip-or-take recurrence with two rolling values.
213.cost: O(n) time and O(1) space. The single-house case must be handled before splitting ranges.

746.title: Min Cost Climbing Stairs
746.prompt: Pay the cost of a stair when stepping from it; begin at stair 0 or 1 and reach just past the last stair with one- or two-step moves.
hints: Define the state as cost to reach a boundary, before paying to leave that stair.
Reaching i comes from paying cost[i−1] or cost[i−2].
746.approach: The starting boundaries 0 and 1 cost zero. For each later boundary choose the cheaper of the two previous reach costs plus the corresponding departure fee.
746.cost: O(n) time and O(1) space; original input contains at least two stairs.

118.title: Pascal's Triangle
118.prompt: Generate the first numRows rows of Pascal’s triangle.
hints: Boundary entries equal one.
Every interior entry adds the two entries above it.
118.approach: Build each row after the previous row. An interior column c combines previous[c−1] and previous[c], giving the binomial recurrence.
118.cost: O(r²) time and output space for r rows; values fit int for the original row limit.

120.title: Triangle
120.prompt: Find the minimum top-to-bottom sum in a triangle, moving to the same or next column of the following row.
hints: A cell’s best suffix path depends on its two children.
Process from the bottom using a rolling row.
120.approach: Before a row update, dp[c] stores the best suffix cost from the row below. Updating columns left-to-right reads old dp[c] and old dp[c+1], which have not both been overwritten.
120.cost: O(r²) time and O(r) extra space for r rows. The input triangle is unchanged.

221.title: Maximal Square
221.prompt: Find the area of the largest all-ones square in a binary character matrix.
hints: A square ending at a cell requires compatible squares above, left, and diagonally above-left.
Its side is one plus the smallest of those three sides.
221.approach: dp[c] stores the largest side ending above the current cell, while dp[c−1] has been updated to the current row. Save the old diagonal before overwriting and track the largest side, then square it for area.
221.cost: O(RC) time and O(C) space. Reset zero cells to zero so stale previous-row squares cannot pass through them.

97.title: Interleaving String
97.prompt: Determine whether s3 interleaves all of s1 and s2 while preserving the order within each source.
97.example: aabcc + dbbca can form aadbbcbcac → true
hints: A state records how many characters were consumed from each source.
The last output character must come from the corresponding last character of one source.
97.approach: dp[i][j] asks whether the first i+j output characters can be formed from prefixes of lengths i and j. Either consume the matching next character from s1 or from s2.
97.cost: O(mn+m+n) time and O((m+1)(n+1)) space; a rolling row reduces memory to O(n).

115.title: Distinct Subsequences
115.prompt: Count how many index-selected subsequences of s equal t; different chosen positions count separately.
hints: A matching character can either be skipped or used as the final target character.
Scan target lengths backward so one source character is not reused.
115.approach: dp[j] counts ways to form the first j target characters from the processed source prefix. On a match, add the ways for j−1 from before the current source character. BigInteger keeps intermediate counts exact even when an irrelevant prefix count is large.
115.cost: O(mn·b) bit-operation upper bound and O(n·b) bits of numeric state for m=|s|, n=|t| and maximum intermediate bit length b (at most O(m)). The final answer is guaranteed to fit int.

10.title: Regular Expression Matching
10.prompt: Match an entire string against a pattern where dot matches any character and star repeats the preceding element zero or more times.
hints: This is not wildcard glob matching: star modifies the preceding token.
For x*, either omit that pair or consume one matching character while keeping the same pattern prefix.
10.approach: dp[i][j] matches text prefix i with pattern prefix j. A star uses dp[i][j−2] for zero copies or dp[i−1][j] for an additional matching copy. Ordinary tokens use the diagonal state.
10.cost: O(mn+m+n) time and O((m+1)(n+1)) space. Patterns are valid: every star has a preceding non-star token.

279.title: Perfect Squares
279.prompt: Return the fewest positive perfect squares summing to n.
hints: Treat square values as reusable coin denominations.
For each total, choose its final square and improve the smaller total’s answer.
279.approach: dp[sum] minimizes one plus dp[sum−square] over all square values that fit. Initializing dp[sum]=sum represents using only ones.
279.cost: O(n√n) time and O(n) space. Root multiplication is safe under the original n limit.

494.title: Target Sum
494.prompt: Assign plus or minus to every nonnegative number and count assignments evaluating to target.
hints: If positive-index values total P and negative-index values total N, P+N=sum and P−N=target.
Count subsets totaling (sum+target)/2, using each occurrence once.
494.approach: Reject unreachable magnitude or odd parity first. A downward 0/1 counting DP chooses which positions get a plus sign. Zero values correctly double counts because plus-zero and minus-zero are distinct assignments.
494.cost: O(nS) time and O(S) space for S=(sum+target)/2; pseudo-polynomial. Counts fit int for the original n<=20 limit.

122.title: Best Time to Buy and Sell Stock II
122.prompt: Maximize stock profit with any number of buy/sell transactions while holding at most one share.
hints: Without fees or cooldown, an upward run can be split into daily gains.
Add every positive difference between neighboring days.
122.approach: Profit over a rising run telescopes into its positive day-to-day differences. Skipping every negative difference and collecting every positive one matches an optimal sequence of transactions.
122.cost: O(n) time and O(1) space. Fees, cooldowns, or transaction limits invalidate this unrestricted decomposition.

123.title: Best Time to Buy and Sell Stock III
123.prompt: Maximize stock profit using at most two completed transactions, holding at most one share.
hints: Keep separate states after the first buy/sell and second buy/sell.
Each state either rests or performs its next legal action from the previous day.
