123.approach: The four states preserve how many transactions may have been used and whether a share is held. Compute next values from old states so every transition has a clear day boundary.
123.cost: O(n) time and O(1) space. Zero sell states represent using fewer than the allowed transactions; sentinel arithmetic is safe under the original price limits.

188.title: Best Time to Buy and Sell Stock IV
188.prompt: Maximize stock profit using at most k transactions, with at most one share held at a time.
hints: Generalize buy/sell states by the number of permitted completed transactions.
Scan transaction counts downward so a buy reads the previous day’s lower-count cash state.
188.approach: cash[t] is the best nonholding profit with at most t sales; hold[t] is the best held-share balance before a possible tth sale. A downward loop keeps dependencies from the previous day. Large k permits the unlimited-transactions shortcut.
188.cost: O(nk) time and O(k) space in the bounded case; O(n) time and O(1) space when k>=n/2.

309.title: Best Time to Buy And Sell Stock With Cooldown
309.prompt: Maximize stock profit with unlimited transactions but one full cooldown day after selling before buying again.
hints: Distinguish resting from having sold today.
A new buy can use yesterday’s rest state, not yesterday’s sold state.
309.approach: Track holding, sold-today, and resting balances. Selling comes from holding; resting can follow rest or sold; buying comes only from rest, which enforces the cooldown.
309.cost: O(n) time and O(1) space. Return only nonholding states.

312.title: Burst Balloons
312.prompt: Burst every balloon to maximize coins; bursting one earns its value times the values of its current neighbors, with virtual boundary values one.
hints: Choosing the first balloon changes both neighbors and entangles subproblems.
Choose the last balloon inside an interval so its two outside neighbors are fixed.
312.approach: Pad values with ones. If k is last in [left,right], all other balloons inside are gone, so its gain uses values[left−1] and values[right+1]. The left and right intervals can then be optimized independently.
312.cost: O(n³) time and O(n²) space. This is an interval-DP extension: subproblems are ranges, not capacities. int scores fit the original limits.

45.title: Jump Game II
45.prompt: Return the minimum jumps to the last index when each value is the maximum allowed forward jump; reachability is guaranteed.
hints: All indices reachable with the current jump count form one frontier range.
Scan that range to find the farthest endpoint for the next jump.
45.approach: currentEnd bounds positions reachable with the existing jump count. Accumulate farthest from every position in that layer; when the scan reaches currentEnd, commit one jump and advance the frontier.
45.cost: O(n) time and O(1) space. This implicit BFS layer scan relies on guaranteed reachability.

134.title: Gas Station
134.prompt: Find a starting gas station allowing one full circular trip, or -1 if impossible; gas and travel costs are nonnegative.
hints: If total gas is below total cost, no start can work.
When a candidate’s running tank becomes negative, every start since that candidate can be discarded.
134.approach: A failed segment has negative total balance. Any later start inside it drops an earlier nonnegative prefix and therefore also fails before or at the same endpoint. Restart after the failed segment, then use total balance to certify the final candidate.
134.cost: O(n) time and O(1) space. Input is nonempty; sums fit int under original bounds.

135.title: Candy
135.prompt: Give each child at least one candy; a child with a higher rating than an adjacent child must receive more. Minimize total candies.
hints: Left-neighbor and right-neighbor constraints can be handled in separate passes.
Use the maximum required candy count from the two directions.
135.approach: A left-to-right pass enforces increases over the left neighbor. A backward pass raises counts when needed for the right neighbor without weakening the first constraint. Every assignment meets the smallest lower bounds from both sides.
135.cost: O(n) time and O(n) space; total fits int under original bounds.

169.title: Majority Element
169.prompt: Find the value appearing more than n/2 times in a nonempty array; its existence is guaranteed.
hints: Cancel pairs of different values.
A strict majority survives all such cancellations.
169.approach: Boyer–Moore voting maintains a candidate and uncanceled balance. A differing value cancels one candidate occurrence; when the balance reaches zero, the next value can become the candidate.
169.cost: O(n) time and O(1) space. Without the guaranteed majority, a second pass must verify the candidate.

678.title: Valid Parenthesis String
678.prompt: Validate parentheses where each star may stand for an opener, a closer, or the empty string.
hints: A prefix may have several possible counts of unmatched openers.
Keep the smallest and largest feasible counts instead of enumerating star choices.
678.approach: Update an interval of possible balances. A closing parenthesis reduces both ends; a star can reduce the minimum or increase the maximum. Clamp the minimum to zero, reject a negative maximum, and accept when zero remains possible at the end.
678.cost: O(n) time and O(n) temporary toCharArray space in this implementation; the balance state is O(1), and a charAt loop removes the allocation.

763.title: Partition Labels
763.prompt: Partition a lowercase string into as many segments as possible so each letter occurs in only one segment.
hints: Any letter already seen forces the current segment to include its last occurrence.
Track the farthest last occurrence among letters in the current segment.
763.approach: The running end is the earliest boundary satisfying all current letters. Once the scan reaches it, closing immediately is safe and maximizes the number of partitions.
763.cost: O(n) time and O(1) auxiliary space for the fixed alphabet, plus output.

846.title: Hand of Straights
846.prompt: Partition all cards into equal-size groups of consecutive values.
hints: The smallest remaining card cannot appear in the middle of a group.
It must begin a group containing each of the next groupSize−1 values.
846.approach: Use an ordered frequency map. Repeatedly start at the smallest remaining key and consume one consecutive run. A missing required value makes every possible grouping fail.
846.cost: O(n log(n+1)) time and O(n) space. Positive group size and original card bounds keep additions safe.

1899.title: Merge Triplets to Form Target Triplet
1899.prompt: Merge triplets with componentwise maximum; determine whether some sequence can produce the target triplet.
hints: Any triplet exceeding the target in one component can never be used.
Among safe triplets, each target component only needs one witness.
1899.approach: Componentwise maxima never decrease, so unsafe triplets are excluded. Combining every safe triplet reaches the target exactly when every component attains its target value somewhere.
1899.cost: O(n) time and O(1) space; the triplet dimension is fixed.

6.title: Zigzag Conversion
6.prompt: Lay out a string by moving down and diagonally up across numRows, then read rows in order.
hints: You only need each character’s destination row, not a full character matrix.
Reverse vertical direction at the first and last rows.
6.approach: Append characters to row builders while bouncing the row index between the two boundaries. Concatenating row buffers reproduces the zigzag reading order.
6.cost: O(n) time and O(n) builder/output space. This is row simulation, not grid DP.

7.title: Reverse Integer
7.prompt: Reverse a signed 32-bit integer’s decimal digits, returning zero if the reversed result is outside int range; do not use a wider integer type.
hints: Appending a digit multiplies the current result by ten first.
Check the quotient and final allowed digit before multiplication, including negative bounds.
7.approach: Pop digits with division and remainder. Before result*10+digit, compare against the positive or negative boundary quotient; the remaining endpoint digits are 7 and -8.
7.cost: O(d) time for d decimal digits and O(1) space; d<=10 for Java int.

9.title: Palindrome Number
9.prompt: Determine whether a signed integer reads the same backward in decimal without converting it to a string.
hints: Negative numbers and nonzero numbers ending in zero cannot qualify.
Reverse only half the digits, then compare the halves.
9.approach: Stop when the reversed suffix reaches or exceeds the remaining prefix. Equal halves represent an even-length palindrome; discarding the reversed half’s middle digit handles odd lengths.
9.cost: O(d) time and O(1) space. Reversing only half avoids overflow from reversing a full int.

12.title: Integer to Roman
12.prompt: Convert an integer from 1 through 3999 to standard Roman numerals.
hints: Include subtractive symbols such as CM, XC, and IV as explicit denominations.
Consume the largest representation unit that fits.
12.approach: A descending table including the six subtractive pairs directly encodes canonical Roman notation. Repeatedly append and subtract each denomination before moving to smaller ones.
12.cost: O(1) bounded work and space for inputs 1..3999; equivalently proportional to the bounded output length. The rule relies on this specific numeral system.

13.title: Roman to Integer
13.prompt: Convert a valid canonical Roman numeral into an integer.
hints: A smaller symbol before a larger one contributes negatively.
Compare each symbol with its next symbol before adding its value.
13.approach: In valid Roman notation, the first symbol of a subtractive pair is exactly a symbol smaller than its successor. Subtract it and add all other symbols.
13.cost: O(n) time and O(1) space. This converts valid input; it is not a complete validator for Roman grammar.

43.title: Multiply Strings
43.prompt: Multiply two nonnegative decimal strings without converting them to built-in integer or arbitrary-precision numeric values.
hints: A digit pair contributes to positions i+j and i+j+1 of a product array.
Accumulate each product into the low slot and carry to the preceding slot.
43.approach: Grade-school multiplication combines every pair of digits. The lower product position is normalized immediately, carrying to the next position; after all pairs, skip leading zeros when formatting.
43.cost: O(mn) time and O(m+n) space for operand lengths m,n; the algorithm avoids numeric parsing of entire strings.

50.title: Pow(x, n)
50.prompt: Compute x raised to signed int exponent n efficiently.
hints: Use the binary representation of the exponent.
Square the base each step and multiply the answer when the current low bit is one.
50.approach: Convert the exponent to long before negating so Integer.MIN_VALUE is representable. A negative exponent inverts the base; binary exponentiation consumes one bit per iteration.
50.cost: O(log(|n|+1)) multiplications and O(1) space. Floating-point rounding applies; input excludes undefined zero-to-negative cases.

66.title: Plus One
66.prompt: Add one to an array of most-significant-first decimal digits.
hints: Carry travels backward from the least significant digit.
A non-nine absorbs the carry; a nine becomes zero and propagates it.
66.approach: Scan right-to-left. The first digit below nine can be incremented and returned immediately. If every digit was nine, allocate the one-longer representation beginning with one.
66.cost: O(n) worst-case time, O(1) auxiliary state and up to O(n) returned-array space. Mutates the input digits even when allocating a new result.

67.title: Add Binary
67.prompt: Add two binary strings and return their binary sum without numeric parsing of the full operands.
hints: Process bits from right to left with one carry.
Emit sum modulo two and carry sum divided by two.
67.approach: The digit sum contains at most two input bits and one carry. Append low bits in reverse order and reverse the builder once after the scan.

137.title: Single Number II
137.prompt: Every int appears three times except one appearing once; find that value using constant extra space.
hints: Pairwise XOR does not cancel triples.
For each bit, take its total set-bit count modulo three.
137.approach: Every tripled value contributes a multiple of three to each bit count. The remainders reconstruct the singleton’s full 32-bit pattern, including its sign bit.
137.cost: O(32n)=O(n) time and O(1) space for fixed-width ints. Unsigned shifts expose negative values’ bits correctly.

172.title: Factorial Trailing Zeroes
172.prompt: Return the number of trailing decimal zeros in n! without constructing the factorial.
hints: Every trailing zero consumes a factor pair 2×5.
Factors of five are scarcer; multiples of 25 contribute a second five.
172.approach: Sum floor(n/5), floor(n/25), and further powers. Repeatedly dividing n by five computes these contributions without risking overflow from multiplying powers.
172.cost: O(log₅(n+1)) time and O(1) space. The method counts factors rather than explicitly multiplying factorial terms.

190.title: Reverse Bits
190.prompt: Reverse all 32 bits of an integer’s bit pattern, including leading zeros.
hints: Always process exactly 32 positions.
Shift the answer left and append the current input low bit; shift input right with zero fill.
190.approach: Each loop transfers one low input bit to the next output position. A fixed iteration count ensures leading input zeros become trailing output zeros.
190.cost: O(32)=O(1) time and O(1) space for Java int. Returned signed int represents the required unsigned 32-bit pattern.

201.title: Bitwise AND of Numbers Range
201.prompt: Compute the bitwise AND of every integer in an inclusive nonnegative range [left,right].
hints: Any changing low bit becomes zero somewhere in the range.
The result is the common binary prefix of both endpoints followed by zeros.
201.approach: Shift both endpoints until they agree, counting shifts. Every removed low position varied within the original interval and cannot survive AND; restore only the common prefix.
201.cost: O(32)=O(1) time and O(1) space under nonnegative int bounds.

268.title: Missing Number
268.prompt: An array of n distinct numbers drawn from 0 through n omits one number. Return it.
hints: Every present value should cancel against the full expected range.
XOR the indices, values, and the final n value.
268.approach: The complete 0..n range contains each expected value once. XOR with the input cancels every present number, leaving only the missing one without sum overflow.
268.cost: O(n) time and O(1) space; distinctness and the exact 0..n domain are essential.

371.title: Sum of Two Integers
371.prompt: Return the sum of two integers without using the addition or subtraction operators.
hints: XOR adds bit positions without carrying.
AND identifies carry positions; shift those carries left and repeat.
371.approach: At each step, a^b is the carry-free sum and (a&b)<<1 is the unresolved carry. Repeat until no carry remains; Java’s fixed-width representation also handles negative operands.
371.cost: At most 32 carry-propagation rounds, so O(1) time and space for Java int. Arithmetic follows fixed-width two’s-complement behavior.

48.title: Rotate Image
48.prompt: Rotate a square matrix clockwise by 90 degrees in place.
hints: A clockwise rotation maps (r,c) to (c,n−1−r).
Transpose, then reverse each row.
48.approach: Transposition swaps row and column coordinates. Reversing each row supplies the remaining horizontal reflection, producing the desired coordinate mapping without another matrix.
48.cost: O(n²) time and O(1) extra space. This is a matrix-transformation extension, not a DP recurrence.

54.title: Spiral Matrix
54.prompt: Read a rectangular matrix in clockwise spiral order.
hints: Maintain the four boundaries of the unread rectangle.
After consuming a side, shrink its boundary and recheck whether the opposite side still exists.
54.approach: Traverse top, right, bottom, and left boundaries in order. Guards before the bottom and left traversals prevent a single row or column from being emitted twice.
54.cost: O(RC) time, O(1) boundary state, and O(RC) output space. Input is unchanged.

73.title: Set Matrix Zeroes
73.prompt: If any matrix cell is zero, set its entire row and column to zero using constant extra space.
hints: Writing zeros immediately can create false new triggers.
Use the first row and column as markers, while separately remembering whether they originally contained zeros.
73.approach: Record original first-row/column flags, then mark interior zeros on those borders. Apply markers only to interior cells before finally clearing the first row or column according to their saved flags.
73.cost: O(RC) time and O(1) extra space; the input matrix doubles as marker storage.

289.title: Game of Life
289.prompt: Advance a binary Game of Life board by one simultaneous generation using the eight-neighbor rules.
289.example: A vertical three-cell blinker becomes a horizontal three-cell blinker.
hints: Neighbor counts must read old states even after some cells are updated.
Keep the old state in bit zero and write the next state into bit one.
289.approach: The low bit remains unchanged during the first pass. Set the second bit when a cell survives with two live neighbors or is born/survives with three. Shift every cell right once to commit the generation.
289.cost: O(RC) time and O(1) extra space. Two bits per cell preserve simultaneity without copying the board.

68.title: Text Justification
68.prompt: Pack words greedily into fixed-width lines. Fully justify nonfinal lines with extra spaces toward the left; left-justify the final line.
hints: First decide which words fit; only then distribute spaces.
Split total spaces evenly among gaps and assign the remainder to earlier gaps; final or one-word lines use single gaps and trailing padding.
68.approach: Greedy packing maximizes words on each line according to the specification. For ordinary lines, quotient/remainder division distributes all remaining columns across gaps. Handle the last line and single-word lines separately.
68.cost: O(total output characters) time and space, plus word-boundary bookkeeping. Every input word is nonempty and no longer than maxWidth.
